title: Good company (205–208)
hook: to see the noble is good; follow the wise as the moon follows the path of the stars

segments.voice: Yesterday, contentment is wealth: health the greatest gift, enough the best riches. Your line was contentment is wealth. What did you name as already enough? Day one hundred ninety-eight.

Think of someone you always feel a little better after seeing. Not because they flatter you. Maybe they're just steady. They listen all the way to the end of your sentence. They don't gossip, and somehow around them you don't either. You leave the coffee with them standing a bit straighter. Now think of someone who has the opposite effect. You know exactly who. We become, slowly, like the people we spend our hours with. Chapter fifteen ends with that simple and slightly uncomfortable truth. Today: good company.
screen: `SOMEONE YOU FEEL BETTER AFTER SEEING.` → `AND SOMEONE WHO'S THE OPPOSITE.` → `WE BECOME OUR COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Verse two oh six, in Max Müller's translation: "The sight of the elect (Arya) is good, to live with them is always happiness". Ariya means noble, not by birth but by character: someone well along the path. Just seeing such a person, the verse says, is good. Then verse two oh seven: "company with the wise is pleasure, like meeting with kinsfolk." Like coming home to family. And the closing image, verse two oh eight: "one ought to follow a good and wise man, as the moon follows the path of the stars." In old India, the moon's path through the sky was traced along a ring of star groups, the lunar mansions. The moon doesn't wander at random; it keeps to a known road. Good friends are that road. The Buddha put this more strongly than you might expect. In one discourse, his attendant Ānanda says that good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrects him: not half. It's the whole of the holy life. The Pali phrase is kalyāṇamitta, a lovely friend, a good friend, someone whose company leans you toward the good. The verses also say that time with fools is painful, and that's worth reading carefully. Buddhists don't take it as permission to look down on anyone. It's about whose habits you're soaking in, day after day, and choosing on purpose. Because you will soak something in. The only question is what.
screen: `ARIYA — NOBLE BY CHARACTER.` · `LIKE MEETING FAMILY.` · `THE MOON FOLLOWS THE STARS.` · `NOT HALF: THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `KEEP GOOD COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind one good person in your life. Not perfect: good. Someone whose company leans you toward patience or honesty or kindness. Picture their face, the way they sound. Let yourself feel glad they exist. If you like, silently wish them well: may you be happy, may you be safe. Then ask one small question: when could I spend a little time with them this week? A call, a walk, a message. Hold that plan lightly, and rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Good company. Verse two oh eight: follow the good and the wise, as the moon follows the path of the stars.
Your line: keep good company. Today, spend a few minutes with a good person, in person or on the phone, and notice how you feel afterward. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists place great weight on kalyāṇamitta, good spiritual friendship, through teachers, the monastic community and fellow practitioners, and many see visiting a respected monk or nun as a blessing in itself.

match.prompt: match each piece of today's verses.
pairs: follows the path of the stars
a good friend on the path

myth: the Buddha said good friendship is half of the holy life
that was Ānanda's guess. the Buddha said it is the whole of it.
in the verse, ariya means noble by birth
it means noble by character: someone well along the path.
verse 207 compares company with the wise to meeting family

fork.setup: you're Ānanda. you tell the Buddha: good friendship must be half of the holy life. what does he answer?
options: not half: it is the whole of the holy life.
fork.reveal: he corrected him: good friendship, kalyāṇamittatā, is the whole of the holy life.

original.note: Pali: a good friend, a lovely friend — someone whose company leans you toward the good.

trapdoor: what you thought: choose nice friends.
what it means: we absorb the company we keep, so keeping good company is a practice in itself.
what a scholar hears: in the Upaḍḍha Sutta (SN 45.2) the Buddha calls good friendship the whole of the holy life; the moon's path runs through the nakkhatta, the lunar mansions.
